title: Data Modeling and Design

toc.title: Business Drivers — 4 Reasons Data Models are Critical
4 Types of Data That Can Be Modeled
Data Model Components — 4 Basic Building Blocks
Three Levels of Detail — ANSI SPARC 1975
Data Model Scorecard® — 10 Categories (100 points total)

html:
1Core Definition and Goal

Definition: Data modeling is the process of discovering, analyzing, and scoping data requirements, and then representing and communicating these data requirements in a precise form called the data model. This process is iterative and may include a conceptual, logical, and physical model.

Goal: To confirm and document an understanding of different perspectives, which leads to applications that more closely align with current and future business requirements, and creates a foundation to successfully complete broad-scoped initiatives such as MDM and data governance programs.

Data models are an important form of Metadata. Proper data modeling leads to lower support costs and increases reusability.

2Business Drivers — 4 Reasons Data Models are Critical

  1. Provide a common vocabulary around data
  2. Capture and document explicit knowledge about an organization's data and systems
  3. Serve as a primary communications tool during projects
  4. Provide the starting point for customization, integration, or replacement of an application

3What Confirming Perspectives Facilitates — 3 Values

  1. Formalization — Concise definition of data structures/relationships; reduces data anomalies; makes data easier to consume
  2. Scope definition — Explains boundaries for data context and implementation of projects, packages, or systems
  3. Knowledge retention/documentation — Preserves corporate memory; reusable map for future projects ("the modeler enables others to understand an information landscape")

44 Types of Data That Can Be Modeled

Type Description IT Alias
Category information Data used to classify and assign types (customer segments, product types) —
Resource information Basic profiles of operational resources: Product, Customer, Supplier, Facility, Organization, Account Reference Data
Business event information Data created while operational processes are in progress: Orders, Invoices, Withdrawals, Meetings Transactional data
Detail transaction information High-volume data from POS systems, social media, sensors, GPS, RFID — can be aggregated/analyzed Big Data

These types refer to "data at rest." Data in motion (messaging, event-based systems) can also be modeled.

5Data Model Components — 4 Basic Building Blocks

Entities, Relationships, Attributes, Domains

Entity

  • A thing about which an organization collects information — the "nouns" of an organization
  • Answers fundamental questions: Who, What, When, Where, Why, How, or Measurement
Category Question Examples
Who Person/org important to business Employee, Customer, Patient
What Product/service the enterprise makes Product, Service, Course
When Calendar/time interval Date, Month, Quarter, Semester
Where Location (actual or electronic) Address, URL, IP Address
Why Event/transaction that keeps business afloat Order, Return, Claim
How Documentation of events Invoice, Contract, Purchase Order
Measurement Counts, sums at/over time Sales, Balance, Item Count

Entity aliases by scheme:

  • Relational → entity
  • Dimensional → dimension / fact table
  • Object-Oriented → class / object
  • Time-Based → hub, satellite, link
  • NoSQL → document / node

Entity aliases by level:

  • Conceptual → concept or term
  • Logical → entity
  • Physical → table (most common)

3 Characteristics of High-Quality Entity Definitions:

  1. Clarity — Easy to read; no obscure acronyms or ambiguous terms
  2. Accuracy — Precise and correct; reviewed by business experts
  3. Completeness — All parts present (examples for codes, scope of uniqueness for identifiers)

Relationship

  • An association between entities (Chen, 1976)
  • Captures interactions and constraints between entities
  • Cardinality — how many of one entity participates with how many of the other: zero, one, or many on each side
  • Represented by foreign keys in relational databases

Relationship Arity:

Type Entities Involved Notes
Unary (Recursive) 1 entity (self-referencing) One-to-many = hierarchy; many-to-many = network
Binary 2 entities Most common on traditional data model diagrams
Ternary 3 entities Three entities in one relationship

Identifying vs. Non-Identifying Relationships:

  • Independent entity: Primary key contains only its own attributes (rectangle)
  • Dependent entity: Primary key contains at least one attribute from another entity (rounded rectangle)
  • Identifying relationship: Parent PK migrated as FK into child's PK
  • Non-identifying relationship: Parent PK migrated as non-primary FK to child

Attribute

  • A property that identifies, describes, or measures an entity
  • Physical equivalent: column, field, tag, or node

Key Types by Construction:

Key Definition
Simple key ONE attribute uniquely identifying an instance (e.g., UPC, VIN)
Surrogate key System-generated integer; no business meaning; not visible to users; used for technical functions
Compound key TWO or more attributes together uniquely identifying an instance
Composite key Contains one compound key + at least one other simple/compound key or non-key attribute

Key Types by Function:

Key Definition
Super key ANY set of attributes that uniquely identifies an entity instance
Candidate key MINIMAL set that uniquely identifies an instance (no subset can uniquely identify)
Primary key The candidate key CHOSEN as the unique identifier
Alternate key A candidate key NOT chosen as PK; still used to find specific instances
Business key (natural key) One or more attributes a business person uses to retrieve a single instance

Surrogate keys and business keys are mutually exclusive.

Domain

  • The complete set of possible values an attribute can be assigned
  • 5 ways domains are defined:
    1. Data Type — Integer, Character(30), Date
    2. Data Format — Templates/masks (postal codes, phone numbers)
    3. List — Finite set of values (e.g., {Open, Shipped, Closed, Returned})
    4. Range — All values between min/max (e.g., OrderDeliveryDate between OrderDate and 3 months future)
    5. Rule-based — Values must comply with a rule (e.g., ItemPrice > ItemCost)

6Six Modeling Schemes

Scheme Notations Notes
Relational IE (most common), IDEF1X, Barker, Chen Dr. Edward Codd, 1970; "one fact in one place"; removes redundancy; ideal for operational systems
Dimensional Dimensional / Axis notation General Mills + Dartmouth, 1960s; fact tables + dimension tables; optimized for query/analysis
Object-Oriented UML class diagram Has classes, attributes, AND operations/methods (not in ER)
Fact-Based ORM/ORM2, FCO-IM Terry Halpin formalized ORM as first-order logic, 1989; no attributes; natural language verbalization
Time-Based Data Vault, Anchor Modeling Data Vault: hubs, links, satellites; Anchor: anchors, attributes, ties, knots
NoSQL Document, Column, Key-Value, Graph Physical-only modeling technique (PDM only)

Relational Key Facts

  • IE notation (Information Engineering): "crow's feet" / tridents to depict cardinality — most common
  • Design objective: Exact expression of business data + one fact in one place (removal of redundancy)
  • Ideal for operational systems (fast data entry, accurate storage)

Dimensional Key Facts

  • Fact tables: Rows are numeric measurements; take up ~90% of database space; large row counts
  • Dimension tables: Textual descriptions; primary source for "query by/report by"; ~10% of data; highly denormalized
  • Grain: The meaning/description of a single row in a fact table — one of the key steps in dimensional design
  • Snowflaking: Normalizing a flat dimensional structure (star schema) into hierarchical/network structures
  • Conformed Dimensions: Built for entire org; shared across dimensional models; consistent terminology and values
  • Conformed Facts: Standardized definitions of terms across individual data marts

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) — 3 Types (ORC):

Type Name Action
Type 1 Overwrite New value overwrites old value in place
Type 2 New Row New values in a new row; old row marked as not current
Type 3 New Column Multiple instances listed in columns on the same row

Star Schema vs. Snowflake:

  • Star Schema: All dimensions collapsed (denormalized) into single structure per dimension
  • Snowflake: Dimensions not collapsed (normalized dimension tables)

Data Vault (Time-Based) — 3 Entity Types

  1. Hubs — Represent primary keys / main business concepts
  2. Links — Transaction integration between hubs
  3. Satellites — Context / descriptive information for hubs; support varying history types

Anchor Modeling — 4 Concepts

  1. Anchors — Model entities and events
  2. Attributes — Model properties of anchors
  3. Ties — Model relationships between anchors
  4. Knots — Model shared properties (e.g., states)

NoSQL — 4 Types

Type Key Characteristic
Document Stores complete business subject in one document structure
Key-Value Two columns only: 'key' and 'value'; value can hold simple or complex data
Column-oriented Closest to RDBMS; stores each column in its own structure; handles complex data types
Graph Best for data whose relations are well represented as nodes with undetermined connections

7Three Levels of Detail — ANSI SPARC 1975

The ANSI SPARC three-schema approach (1975): Conceptual, External (→ Logical), Internal (→ Physical)

Level Type Description Independence
Conceptual (CDM) Requirements planning High-level; basic/critical entities and relationships; captures scope and key terminology Technology-independent
Logical (LDM) Requirements analysis Detailed representation; adds attributes; applies normalization; captures business rules (relational) or business questions (dimensional) Technology-independent
Physical (PDM) Design activity Technical solution for specific technology; denormalization, indexing, partitioning Technology-specific

CDM + LDM = requirements planning and analysis. PDM = design activity.

Physical Model Variants

  • Canonical Model: Data in motion between systems (web services, ESB, EAI); designed to be generic for reuse
  • Views: Virtual tables; simplify queries, control access, rename columns without redundancy/referential integrity issues
    • Standard view: runs SQL at query time
    • Materialized (instantiated) view: runs at predetermined time
  • Partitioning: Splitting a table
    • Vertical: Separating groups of columns
    • Horizontal: Separating groups of rows (e.g., regional customer tables)
  • Denormalization: Deliberate redundancy to improve performance or enforce security; Star Schema (dimensional) = fully denormalized

8Normalization — 6 Normal Forms

Purpose: Organize business complexity into stable data structures; keep each attribute in only one place to eliminate redundancy.

Normal Form Rule
1NF Valid PK; every attribute depends on the PK; removes repeating groups; attributes are atomic; resolves many-to-many with associative entities
2NF Minimal PK; every attribute depends on the complete primary key
3NF No hidden PKs; every attribute depends on "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key"
BCNF Resolves overlapping composite candidate keys
4NF Resolves all many-to-many-to-many relationships in pairs
5NF Resolves inter-entity dependencies into basic pairs; all join dependencies use parts of primary keys

"Normalized model" usually means 3NF. BCNF, 4NF, and 5NF occur rarely.

9Abstraction

  • Abstraction: Removal of details to broaden applicability while preserving essential properties
  • Generalization: Groups common attributes into supertype entities
  • Specialization: Separates distinguishing attributes into subtype entities
  • Subtyping implies inheritance — subtype inherits all properties from supertype
  • Example: School (supertype) → University and High School (subtypes)

Resolving abstraction at physical level:

  • Subtype absorption: Subtype attributes become nullable columns in the supertype table
  • Supertype partition: Supertype attributes are included in separate tables for each subtype

10Activities — 4

# Activity Phase
2.1 Plan for Data Modeling Planning (P)
2.2 Build the Data Models — CDM, LDM, PDM Development (D)
2.3 Review the Data Models Control (C)
2.4 Manage the Data Models Operations (O)

Forward Engineering vs. Reverse Engineering

Direction Order Purpose
Forward Engineering CDM → LDM → PDM Building a new application from requirements
Reverse Engineering PDM → LDM → CDM Documenting an existing database

PDM Physical Design Steps (8)

  1. Resolve logical abstractions (subtype absorption / supertype partition)
  2. Add attribute details (physical names, data types, lengths, constraints, nullability)
  3. Add reference data objects (separate code table / master shared table / embedded rules)
  4. Assign surrogate keys
  5. Denormalize for performance
  6. Index for performance (alternate access path; avoid full table scans)
  7. Partition for performance (date key recommended for dimensional)
  8. Create views

11Tools — 6 Types

Tool Purpose
Data Modeling Tools Automate modeling tasks; forward/reverse engineering; generate DDL; naming standards validation; Metadata storage
Lineage Tools Capture/maintain source structures per attribute; enable impact analysis; Excel is common but limited
Data Profiling Tools Explore data content; validate against Metadata; identify DQ gaps and anomalies
Metadata Repositories Store descriptive information (diagram + text); enable Metadata integration and exchange
Data Model Patterns Reusable modeling structures — elementary (nuts/bolts), assembly (business building blocks), integration (linking assembly patterns)
Industry Data Models Pre-built for entire industries (healthcare, telecom, insurance, banking, manufacturing); sources: ARTS (retail), SID (communications), ACORD (insurance)

12Naming Conventions Best Practices

  • Standard: ISO 11179 Metadata Registry (international standard for Metadata in organizations)
  • Logical names: Full words, meaningful to business users; avoid all but familiar abbreviations; use blank spaces between words
  • Physical names: Must conform to DBMS max length; use abbreviations where necessary; use underscores between words
  • Class words: Last term in attribute names (e.g., Quantity, Name, Code) — distinguish attributes from entities
  • Names should not reflect environment (test, QA, production)

13Database Design Best Practices — PRISM

Letter Principle Meaning
P Performance and ease of use Quick and easy access for authorized users; maximize business value
R Reusability Multiple applications can use the data; avoid coupling DB to a single application
I Integrity Always valid business meaning; enforce constraints as close to data as possible
S Security Available to authorized users only; enforce security as close to data as possible
M Maintainability Cost of data work should not exceed its value; fastest response to business changes

14Data Model Scorecard® — 10 Categories (100 points total)

# Category Max Score
1 How well does the model capture the requirements? 15
2 How complete is the model? 15
3 How well does the model match its scheme? 10
4 How structurally sound is the model? 15
5 How well does the model leverage generic structures? 10
6 How well does the model follow naming standards? 5
7 How well has the model been arranged for readability? 5
8 How good are the definitions? 10
9 How consistent is the model with the enterprise? 5
10 How well does the metadata match the data? 10
TOTAL 100

Highest-weighted categories: requirements (15), completeness (15), structural soundness (15).

15Data Model Governance

Design Quality Management

Data professionals must balance:

  • Short-term needs (timely data, project delivery) vs. long-term needs (secure, recoverable, sharable, reusable structures)

Design Review Best Practices

  • Conduct with group of subject matter experts representing different backgrounds
  • One leader facilitates; a scribe captures discussion
  • If no approval: modeler reworks; unresolvable issues → owner of the system decides

Model Versioning — Change Tracking Fields

Each change must note: Why, What and How, When (approved + made), Who, Where (in which models)

16Exam Q&A (20 Questions)

Q1. How is data modeling defined in DMBOK2? A: The process of discovering, analyzing, and scoping data requirements, then representing and communicating them in a precise form called the data model. The process is iterative and may include conceptual, logical, and physical models.

Q2. What is the goal of data modeling? A: To confirm and document an understanding of different perspectives, leading to applications that align with business requirements, and creating a foundation to successfully complete initiatives such as MDM and data governance programs.

Q3. What are the 4 business drivers (reasons data models are critical)? A: (1) Common vocabulary; (2) Capture and document explicit knowledge; (3) Primary communications tool; (4) Starting point for customization, integration, or replacement.

Q4. What are the 4 types of data that can be modeled? A: (1) Category information; (2) Resource information (= Reference Data); (3) Business event information (= transactional); (4) Detail transaction information (= Big Data).

Q5. What are the 4 basic building blocks of a data model? A: Entities, Relationships, Attributes, and Domains.

Q6. What are the 3 characteristics of high-quality entity definitions? A: Clarity, Accuracy, Completeness.

Q7. What are the 6 modeling schemes? A: Relational, Dimensional, Object-Oriented, Fact-Based, Time-Based, NoSQL.

Q8. Who developed relational theory and when? What are its two design objectives? A: Dr. Edward Codd in 1970. Design objectives: (1) Exact expression of business data; (2) One fact in one place (removal of redundancy).

Q9. What is a slowly changing dimension, and what are the 3 SCD types? A: A dimension with attributes that change over time, managed by ORC: Type 1 = Overwrite (new value replaces old), Type 2 = New Row (new row added, old row marked inactive), Type 3 = New Column (multiple values in columns on same row).

Q10. What percentage of database space do fact tables typically occupy? And dimension tables? A: Fact tables ≈ 90%. Dimension tables ≈ 10%.

Q11. What is the difference between a Star Schema and a Snowflake? A: Star Schema: all dimensions are collapsed (denormalized) into single tables. Snowflake: dimensions are not collapsed — they remain normalized.

Q12. What are the 3 entity types in a Data Vault model? A: Hubs (primary keys/main concepts), Links (transaction integration between hubs), Satellites (context/descriptive information supporting varying history).

Q13. What are the 4 entity types in Anchor Modeling? A: Anchors (entities/events), Attributes (properties of anchors), Ties (relationships between anchors), Knots (shared properties like states).

Q14. What do the three levels of detail (CDM, LDM, PDM) correspond to in the ANSI SPARC model? A: Conceptual → SPARC Conceptual; Logical → SPARC External; Physical → SPARC Internal. CDM and LDM are requirements planning/analysis; PDM is a design activity.

Q15. What does "normalized model" usually mean? A: Third Normal Form (3NF) — "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key." BCNF, 4NF, and 5NF occur rarely.

Q16. What is the difference between forward engineering and reverse engineering? A: Forward engineering: CDM → LDM → PDM (building a new application from requirements). Reverse engineering: PDM → LDM → CDM (documenting an existing database).

Q17. What does the acronym PRISM stand for in database design best practices? A: Performance and ease of use, Reusability, Integrity, Security, Maintainability.

Q18. What are the 10 categories of the Data Model Scorecard®? A: (1) Captures requirements (15), (2) Completeness (15), (3) Matches scheme (10), (4) Structural soundness (15), (5) Leverages generic structures (10), (6) Naming standards (5), (7) Readability (5), (8) Definitions (10), (9) Enterprise consistency (5), (10) Metadata matches data (10).

Q19. What are conformed dimensions and why do they matter? A: Dimensions built with the entire organization in mind (not just one project) — allowing them to be shared across dimensional models with consistent terminology and values.

Q20. What is the grain of a fact table? A: The meaning or description of a single row of data in the fact table — the most detail any row will have. Defining the grain is one of the key steps in dimensional design.
